> Random Forest applied to a real ATI study: can transcriptomic signatures at
> Week 24 predict which animals rebound after treatment interruption?

## The session

This session works a complete Random Forest pipeline on real RNA-seq data from
an **analytical treatment interruption (ATI)** study. The question is whether
gene expression at Week 24 carries a signal that separates animals which
rebound from those which do not.

## Materials

[{{< fa file-code >}} RF_HIV_Rebound_Analysis.R](RF_HIV_Rebound_Analysis.R){.btn .btn-primary}
[{{< fa table >}} Expression.csv](Expression.csv){.btn .btn-outline-secondary}
[{{< fa table >}} Meta_Data.csv](Meta_Data.csv){.btn .btn-outline-secondary}

Put all three in the same folder, set that folder as your working directory,
and run the script top to bottom.

## The data

| File | Shape | Contents |
|---|---|---|
| `Expression.csv` | 18,280 genes × 20 samples | Raw RNA-seq counts, genes in rows |
| `Meta_Data.csv` | 20 samples | `SampleID`, `Status` (Rebound / NoRebound), `Group`, `SetVL`, and longitudinal plasma viral load from `d10.p.t.i` to `d114.p.t.i` |

::: {.callout-note}
## Read the shape before you read the code
**18,280 features. 20 samples.** Sit with that ratio for a moment — it is the
single most important fact about this dataset, and we return to it below.
:::

## What the script does

1. **Setup** — installs missing packages defensively, one at a time.
2. **QC and PCA** — do the groups separate at all before we model?
3. **Boruta feature selection** — an all-relevant wrapper around Random Forest
   that tests each gene against permuted "shadow" copies of itself.
4. **Random Forest with LOOCV** — leave-one-out cross-validation, because with
   n=20 a held-out test set would be two or three animals.
5. **Ranking and export** — candidate biomarkers with scores and p-values.

::: {.callout-tip}
## A note on installing Boruta
Boruta ≥ 10.0.0 pulls in a dependency that needs a Rust toolchain to compile.
The script handles this — it forces a pre-compiled binary install first, and
falls back to Boruta 9.0.0 (no Rust needed) if no binary exists for your
platform. If you hit a Rust error, you are running the install by hand rather
than letting the script do it.
:::

## The methodological point {#sec-pvsn}

::: {.callout-important}
## 18,280 features, 20 samples
With far more features than samples, *some* gene will separate your groups
perfectly by chance alone. This is not a flaw in Random Forest — it is a
property of the geometry. Any sufficiently flexible model can memorise 20
points.

This is exactly why the script uses **Boruta** (testing each gene against
permuted shadow features, so chance separation has to beat noise) and
**LOOCV** rather than a single train/test split. These are not decoration.
They are what stands between a biomarker and an artifact.
:::

Questions worth holding as you work through the outputs:

1. **Does the ROC look too good?** With n=20, a near-perfect AUC should raise
   your eyebrows, not your confidence.
2. **Would the same genes survive on a different 20 animals?** That is the
   question a reviewer will ask, and this design cannot answer it.
3. **What is the base rate?** How many of the 20 rebound? If the split is
   uneven, accuracy is a misleading summary — see
   [Foundations](../2-ai-application/1-foundations.qmd).
4. **Is `SetVL` doing the work?** Check whether your top genes are proxies for
   set-point viral load rather than independent signal.

## Exercises

1. Run the script end to end. How many genes does Boruta confirm?
2. Re-run with a different `set.seed()`. Do the same genes survive?
3. Take the top gene and plot it against `SetVL`. What do you see?
4. *Discussion.* You have a ranked biomarker table and an ROC curve. What would
   you need before publishing these as correlates of rebound?
